title.title: Quasipolynomial algorithms for mean-payoff games
title.subtitle: Claim: mean-payoff, stochastic and parity games solved deterministically in $2^{O((\log L)^2)}$ bit operations

plain: Two players shove a token round a map of gains and losses; the claim finds who wins far faster than before

beats.text: Two players push a token round a weighted graph and fight over the long-run average
Schematically: binary weights had only subexponential randomized algorithms
Claimed: quasipolynomial, where parity games landed in 2017. P is still open

steps: Give every spot a score; winning spots sit near the top
Ask only which spots are forced high or low
Recurse: halve the range, or reweight the spots
A measure that cannot grow forever caps the recursion

after.label: Claimed, Sep 2026
after.note: deterministic; $L$ is the full binary input length

achievement.note: Quasipolynomial, not polynomial: whether these games are in P stays open

verify.detail: In Lean: the randomized algorithm (success $7/8$) and a counterexample; not the deterministic one
verify.ourCheck: We did not build the Lean or referee the proof

voice.text: Two players fight over the long-run average. Big weights made this slow.
Recursion halves the search range or grows a bounded measure, so it stops.
Claimed: deterministic quasipolynomial time, for all three games.

sources.quote: best binary-weight bounds were subexponential randomized strategy improvement 2^{O(sqrt(n log n))} (Bjorklund-Vorobyov)
Deterministic 2^{O((log(L+2))^2)}-bit-operation algorithms (L = full binary input length)
Quasipolynomial, not polynomial; P membership remains open.

partial formalization: RandomizedMeanPayoff.lean (randomized quasipolynomial algorithm, success 7/8) and TruffetCounterexample.lean; the deterministic, stochastic and parity-extension papers are not formalized
